title: A four-to-three Czech vote raises rates over second-round inflation risks
summary: The Czech National Bank Board raised the two-week repo rate by 25 basis points to 4% on 5 November and moved its other policy rates by the same amount. The decision drew four votes in favour and three for holding rates unchanged. The vote matters because headline inflation had remained close to the 2% target since January 2024 and the Bank had already raised rates in June. A reader of the initial decision knew the size of the increase. The press-conference statement disclosed how narrow the majority was and which risks the Board collectively considered most important.

The majority described the move as protection against second-round effects of a commodity cost shock. Earlier energy increases could be passed through to a wider range of products, change expectations or enter wage claims after the initial effect on fuel had faded. Core inflation was already elevated, with services a major contributor. A tight labour market, rapid wage growth, increasing household consumption and business investment, and strong property prices all supported the concern that firms might sustain price increases. June’s rise and elevated long-term rates had already tightened conditions. The Board reasoned that additional action could anchor expectations and stabilize new lending. It did not publish an estimated effect size for either channel (decision).

The Monetary Department projected average inflation of 2.1% in 2026 and a temporary acceleration around the turn of the year. The statement gives no full-year figure for 2027 inflation. It reduced the 2026 GDP growth forecast from 2.2% to 1.7% and projected 2.5% growth in 2027. The hike therefore came alongside a half-point downgrade to expected current-year growth. Wage-sensitive services, public demand and credit-financed property activity can maintain pressure on domestic prices even while the economy as a whole grows more slowly than previously projected.

Financing conditions supplied another reason the decision was close. Higher longer-term rates could already restrain mortgage or investment financing, even if the overnight policy outlook changed little. On the other hand, faster lending and debt financing of public spending could expand money balances and support expenditures. The statement described material tensions in some overseas sovereign-bond markets, together with the risk of a global correction where government debts were high. A common shock to long bond yields across countries could therefore tighten domestic conditions independently of a revision to the expected CNB rate. The three dissenters’ own detailed reasoning was not given in this press statement (decision and risks).

The Board named the koruna, domestic wages and demand, fiscal policy and the transmission of commodity prices as evidence for coming decisions. It also pointed to weaker activity in parts of the euro area and the possibility of a wider correction in asset prices. Those external developments could dampen Czech inflation, whereas a larger domestic deficit or faster credit and wage growth would push the risk balance the other way. The statement does not attribute an individual argument to any of the three members who preferred to hold. An inference about how close they were to changing their votes requires the minutes or subsequent remarks.

The communications sequence offers a way to test what investors learned. The separate CNB rate bulletin announced a 3 p.m. governor’s press conference and set a 2:30 p.m. accreditation deadline. The deadline does not identify when dealers first saw the policy decision. Establish the actual release timestamps before comparing Czech swap rates and the koruna around the headline, vote split and subsequent commentary. Repricing in a short window could reflect a surprise about the stance today, about the odds of another move, or both. This statement reports the Board’s assessment and contains no market-price observations.

questions.question: How much policy repricing reflected the hike and how much reflected the close vote?
questions.detail: Establish the first reliable timestamp on the rate bulletin, then the publication time for the 3 p.m. conference statement and vote. Compare near-meeting contracts and the koruna in separate windows, controlling for contemporaneous European rates and currency news. If traders expected broad support for a hike, the close vote might alter their expectation of follow-up tightening even after the repo rate rose. Its direction cannot be inferred from the vote alone.

questions.question: Did the cost shock persist outside goods exposed directly to commodity prices?
questions.detail: Track prices in labour-intensive services, wage negotiations and medium-horizon expectations against input-cost changes and exchange rates. Allow for staggered contract resets. A one-time pass-through into final prices differs from repeated revisions extending into sectors with limited direct exposure. Compare the timing of services repricing with the June rise and the November vote. Persistently high wage settlements after energy prices stabilise would matter more for the medium-term decision than a one-off movement in retail fuel.

questions.question: Was the growth downgrade changing the balance between private demand and fiscal activity?
questions.detail: Compare consumption, corporate investment, government expenditure and net trade with the August and November forecast vintages. Relate each to new credit by borrower. A decline in aggregate growth can coexist with persistent domestic pricing pressure if relatively labour-intensive demand or government spending remains strong. Look separately at growth in government borrowing, new household lending and property prices. The outlook explicitly puts those channels alongside weak euro-area demand, so the result can differ even for the same aggregate GDP surprise.
